content: Iodized salt should be made available to and consumed by all individuals in the population older than one year of age. Infants and young children are generally assumed to receive adequate iodine through breast milk or iodine-enriched infant formula, provided these are used as recommended. However, the addition of salt to foods consumed by young children may require regulation to prevent both insufficient and excessive intake of sodium or iodine. Pregnant women have an increased daily iodine requirement of 250 µg/day. If iodine deficiency is identified, additional interventions, such as iodine supplementation, may be necessary. Salt intake is often correlated with caloric intake, and pregnant women typically increase their energy consumption during this physiological stage. Policies aimed at reducing salt intake to less than 5 g/day and ensuring salt iodization are compatible, cost-effective, and beneficial for public health. While salt is an effective vehicle for iodine fortification, promoting iodized salt should not encourage higher salt consumption among the public. Monitoring the quality of food-grade salt is critical to ensure the efficacy and safety of iodine fortification. Additionally, monitoring urinary iodine excretion (UIE) and urinary iodine concentration (UIC) is essential not only to detect iodine deficiency but also to identify excessive iodine intake. This allows for adjustments in iodine fortification levels to prevent health risks associated with iodine excess. Countries should assess iodine losses from iodized salt under local conditions, including production, climate, packaging, and storage. These factors can significantly influence the amount of iodine that needs to be added during production to ensure adequate iodine levels at the household level. The fortification of salt with iodine should be regulated by governments and aligned with other local or national programs to ensure the safe delivery of fortified salt within acceptable dosage ranges. Special attention should be given to identifying barriers to equitable access to iodized salt for all population groups in need. National programs should be culturally appropriate to the target populations to ensure acceptance, adoption, and sustainability. Clear legislation should be established for food producers and distributors, particularly in regions where processed foods and meals consumed outside households are the primary sources of dietary salt. This legislation should address both proper iodization of salt and the salt content in industrialized food products. An efficient system for ongoing and routine data collection, including quality assurance measures and household use of iodized salt, is essential to ensure the effectiveness and sustainability of iodized salt programs. Regular monitoring and evaluation can help identify barriers that limit equal access to fortified salt and address health inequities. Iodine is a trace element essential for the synthesis of thyroid hormones, which are critical for growth, development, and metabolic regulation. The iodine content of foods depends on the iodine levels in the soil. In areas with iodine-deficient soil and water, plants and animals are also iodine-deficient. Populations relying on these food sources require iodine supplementation through interventions such as iodized salt. Women of reproductive age are particularly vulnerable to iodine deficiency, as their neonates are at high risk of irreversible mental impairment if iodine deficiency occurs in utero. Breastfeeding women are another vulnerable group, as breast milk may be the sole source of iodine for infants during the first six months of life. Globally, approximately one-third of the population lives in areas with low natural iodine levels, necessitating permanent iodine-supplying interventions. Around 241 million school-age children worldwide are estimated to have insufficient iodine intake, with the highest numbers in the WHO South-East Asia and African regions. Salt iodization is the preferred strategy for controlling iodine deficiency disorders and has been implemented in over 120 countries. Many nations have successfully eliminated or significantly reduced iodine deficiency disorders through salt iodization and dietary diversification. Dairy products, when derived from cattle fed iodine-enriched feed, are also good sources of iodine and should be included in dietary diversification efforts. The most visible sign of iodine deficiency is goiter, an enlargement of the thyroid gland. Inadequate iodine intake can lead to hypothyroidism, which is associated with a range of iodine deficiency disorders, including impaired brain development, spontaneous abortion, stillbirths, congenital anomalies, and delayed physical development. These disorders can be prevented by ensuring adequate iodine intake. Both insufficient and excessive iodine intake can negatively affect thyroid function. Excessive iodine intake may lead to iodine-induced hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism, particularly in older adults with pre-existing nodular goiter. On a population level, iodine-induced hyperthyroidism is typically a transient condition that resolves with the correction of iodine deficiency. The recommended daily iodine intake varies by age and physiological status: 90 µg/day for infants and children under six years, 120 µg/day for children aged 6–12 years, 150 µg/day for adolescents and adults, and 250 µg/day for pregnant and lactating women. Sea fish and certain seaweeds are good dietary sources of iodine, as are vegetables, cereals, poultry, meat, and milk when produced in iodine-sufficient soils or when animals are given iodine-containing feed supplements. Urinary iodine excretion (UIE) using 24-hour urine collections is the ideal biochemical indicator for assessing iodine status. However, due to practical challenges, alternative indicators may be used in population assessments.
